checks.claim: Paine pried every ochre sea star off a stretch of rock at Mukkaw Bay, Washington, from 1963 on, threw them into the bay, and left an adjacent stretch alone
checks.note: Nautilus: began June 1963, crowbar, hurled them as far as he could into the bay; adjacent stretch left alone. SciAm spells it Makah Bay; same site.

checks.claim: Key: species fell from 15 to 8 within a year, as mussels crowded out the rest
checks.note: Scitable: within a year, fifteen to eight species. SciAm: 'Within a year, the total number of species had halved.' Grokipedia: 15 to 8 within one year. Wikipedia alone dates the count of 8 to three years later, and HHMI gives the starting count as 16; Paine's paper and most sources give 15 to 8, so the key stands. Goose barnacles (Mitella) shared the takeover with mussels; 'the mussels crowded out the rest' is a fair simplification.

checks.claim: Sea stars there eat mostly mussels and barnacles
checks.note: Barnacles were the most numerous prey; mussels and chitons gave the most calories. 'Mostly mussels and barnacles' is a fair grade-level simplification.

checks.claim: Wrong: rose to 22 as prey were spared
checks.note: Wrong in the stem's count of rock-clinging species within a year. (Lafferty and Suchanek 2016 note that mussel beds later shelter many associated species, but that is a different, long-run count.)

checks.claim: Wrong: stayed at 15; wrong: fell to 1 within a year
checks.note: Mussels largely took over only about ten years later (Wikipedia; Nautilus: over five years). Within a year it was 8.

checks.claim: Context: barnacles first, then mussels crowded out seaweeds, limpets, chitons; mussels came close to taking it all only years later
checks.note: Acorn barnacles covered the space within three months; by June 1964 goose barnacles and mussels displaced them; four algae, two limpets and two chitons left; mussels took most space over five years.

checks.claim: Context: Paine named it a keystone species (1969), after the stone that locks an arch together; definition disproportionate to numbers
checks.note: Grokipedia: coined by Paine in 1969, 'the wedge-shaped stone at the apex of an arch that locks the structure in place'. Wikipedia: 1969, The American Naturalist; 'disproportionately large effect ... relative to its abundance'.

checks.claim: Wolves gone about 70 years; 31 wolves from Canada released 1995 and 1996
checks.note: Last wolves killed 1926; 14 from Alberta in 1995, 17 more from Canada in 1996 (Grokipedia: Alberta and British Columbia). Ten more wolves from Montana followed in 1997 by NPS counts, but the stem says only the 31 from Canada, which is true.

checks.claim: Over the next 15 years young willows and aspens along some northern-range streams grew taller
checks.note: Grokipedia: aspen height growth 1998-2010, willow crown volume rising 2001-2020; Ripple and Beschta 2012 'the first 15 years'. 'Some streams' is suitably hedged.

checks.claim: Key (attributed 'by their account'): wolves cut the elk that browsed young shoots
checks.note: Elk are wolves' main prey and browse willow and aspen. Framed as the cascade proponents' account; does not overclaim.

checks.claim: Wrong: beavers, bison, hares cut by wolves
checks.note: Beavers and bison both increased after wolves returned (Ripple and Beschta 2012: bison summer counts 708 to 1,385; beaver colonies 1 to 12). No source credits wolves with cutting hares.

checks.claim: Context: northern-range elk about 16,800 (1995) to about 8,300 (2004)
Context: beavers rose from one colony to nine
checks.note: Wikipedia: one colony in 2001, nine by 2011. Ripple and Beschta 2012 give one (1996) to 12 (2009) on the northern range. Both start at one; 'to nine' is sourced. Optional: 'to nine or more'.

checks.claim: Context: the debate (bears, hunters, hard winter, drought; beavers released north of the park; tallest-aspen sampling exaggerated recovery)
checks.note: Brice, Larsen and MacNulty 2022: sampling the tallest young aspen overstated regeneration; random sampling showed a weaker cascade. NPS beaver page: 129 beavers released north of the park 1986-1999, causes 'topics of intense debate'. Wikipedia lists bears, hunting, winter, drought. Wording reflects the debate honestly.

checks.claim: Killer whales began hunting sea otters off the Aleutians in the 1990s as seals and sea lions grew scarce
checks.note: No attack seen until 1991; Estes linked it to the collapse of seals and sea lions. Grokipedia says the decline ran from the mid/late 1980s, so '1990s' is the first observed attacks; acceptable.

checks.claim: Open-coast otters fell about a quarter each year; held steady in a lagoon the whales could not enter
checks.note: 'declined by about 25 percent each year during the 1990s'; Clam Lagoon, 'inaccessible to killer whales', held steady while Kuluk Bay fell 76 percent.

checks.claim: Key: kelp thinned as urchins multiplied
checks.note: 'Exploding sea urchin populations have decreased kelp densities by a factor of 12.'

checks.claim: Wrong choices (thicker with fewer otters; whales eat urchins; stayed the same)
checks.note: Otters do not eat kelp; transient killer whales take marine mammals, not urchins; kelp fell.

checks.claim: Context: kelp about a twelfth as thick; Clam Lagoon reasoning; Estes led the study
checks.note: Factor of 12; Estes lead author (Estes, Tinker, Williams, Doak, Science 1998).

checks.claim: Context: 'more whales meant less kelp'
checks.note: The whales did not grow more numerous: the study blames a change in what they hunted, and says as few as four killer whales could have caused the otter decline. Fix: 'more hunting by the whales meant less kelp'.

checks.claim: Cane toads brought to Queensland in 1935 to eat cane beetles; skin glands hold a poison that kills many native animals
checks.note: Introduced 1935 (Gordonvale) against cane beetles; bufadienolides in the parotoid glands of the skin.

checks.claim: Ecologists studied a river valley in the Kimberley before and after the toads arrived
checks.note: Doody et al. 2015 (Ecology 96: 2544-2554): a five-year period spanning the toads' invasion of the Kimberley; the sources read do not name the exact river, but the water monitors and pandanus-nesting finches are riverside animals, so the vague 'a river valley' is safe.

checks.claim: Key: more chicks lived as nest-raiding monitor lizards died off
checks.note: Water monitor declines 'approached 50%' over five years, 'apparently causing fledging success of the Crimson Finch ... to increase from 55% to 81%'. Monitors ate eggs and fledglings (phys.org).

checks.claim: Wrong choices (toads ate their insects; poison fouled water; nothing changed)
checks.note: Fledging success rose; none of these is supported.

checks.claim: Context: water monitors fell close to half over five years; fledging success 55 to 81 percent; toads never controlled cane beetles
checks.note: Abstract figures match. Grokipedia: the beetle control 'failed empirically'.

checks.claim: Context: 'An invader with no natural enemies'
checks.note: Overclaim: keelback snakes eat toads without harm and meat ants kill young toads (Grokipedia); Wikipedia says 'no efficient natural predators'. Fix: 'An invader that few native animals can safely eat can thus help one native species by killing its predator, two links away.'

checks.claim: Wild rabbits set loose in Australia for hunting in 1859; spread across much of the continent
checks.note: Thomas Austin, Barwon Park, 1859, 'explicitly for recreational hunting'; over 70% of suitable land by the 1920s.

checks.claim: From 1995 a new rabbit virus cut the rabbits of South Australia's deserts sharply (which virus, where)
checks.note: Rabbit haemorrhagic disease virus (a calicivirus, not myxomatosis, which was 1950) escaped quarantine on Wardang Island, South Australia, in 1995 (official release 1996). Pedler et al. 2016: rabbits fell 85% at one arid SA site and 139 to 22 per km2 at another.

checks.claim: Key: hopping mice spread widely as cats and foxes grew fewer
checks.note: Pedler et al. (Conservation Biology 2016): dusky hopping mouse extent 23 to 105-130 thousand km2, spinifex hopping mouse 180 to 276-356; cat and fox numbers 'followed rabbit population trends'; the authors credit fewer rabbit-dependent predators and less competition.

checks.claim: Wrong choices (scarce from more hunting; virus spread to them; stayed the same)
checks.note: The mice spread; classic RHDV infects only European rabbits.

checks.claim: Context: both ends of the web credited; the virus infects only European rabbits
checks.note: Classic RHDV 'only affects adult European rabbits'. Pedler: 'decreased competition for food resources and declines in rabbit-dependent predators'.

checks.claim: Context: four kinds of small native mammals 'came to cover several times as much of the desert as before'
checks.note: True of three of the four, not of the spinifex hopping mouse, whose extent of occurrence rose only from 180 to 276-356 thousand km2 (1.5 to 2 times; area of occupancy 3 to 7-8). Fix: 'came to cover far more of the desert than before, most of them several times as much.'

checks.claim: Zebra mussels reached North America in ships' ballast water and appeared in the Hudson in 1991
checks.note: Strayer: they 'hitched a ride to Detroit in the ballast water of an ocean-going ship'; first appeared in the Hudson in (May) 1991.

checks.claim: Within two years billions lived on the riverbed; algae fell by four-fifths; shad and herring fewer and slower-growing
checks.note: 50 to 600 billion by 1992; phytoplankton biomass fell 80%; open-water fish (shad, herring) fell in numbers and growth (Strayer).

checks.claim: Key: the link is the tiny animals (zooplankton) the fish feed on
checks.note: Crustacean zooplankton, 'an important food for young fish', were cut in half.

checks.claim: Wrong choices (water plants, sunfish, bigger fish)
checks.note: Shallow-water sunfish increased; clearer water helped plants; neither links the mussels to the open-water fish's decline.

checks.claim: Context: small zooplankton nearly vanished, larger kinds halved; sunfish of the shallows increased; native mussels, once over a billion, disappearing
checks.note: All match Strayer and the Cary page. Optional precision: the small zooplankton (rotifers) vanished mainly because the mussels strained them out too, not only for want of algae; 'with the algae strained out' reads as timing, so not an error. A tweak would be 'small zooplankton, which the mussels strained out as well, nearly vanished'.

checks.claim: McGregor's team put video cameras on feral cats' collars in northern Australia and filmed 101 hunts
checks.note: 23 deployments on 13 cats, 2012-2014, central Kimberley; 'we recorded 101 hunting events, of which 32 were successful'.

checks.claim: GPS-tracked cats walked up to 12 km beyond their home ranges to hunt on freshly burned, intensely burned ground and stayed about two weeks
checks.note: 32 GPS-collared cats; journeys up to 12.5 km; average stay 15 days; cats preferred fires both intense and recent. 'Up to 12' rounds 12.5 down, harmless.

checks.claim: Key: most hunts in open country ended in a kill
checks.note: 'a 70% chance of a kill in an open area, and 17% chance in an area with dense grass or complex rocks'.

checks.claim: Wrong choices (thick grass; rocks; equal on any ground)
checks.note: 17% in dense grass or complex rocks.

checks.claim: Context: 70 vs 17 percent; fire strips cover; researchers suggest fewer intense fires and denser grass and shrubs
checks.note: Authors propose suppressing intense fires, reducing feral herbivores and restoring dense grass or shrubs.

checks.claim: Rinderpest, a cattle disease that also kills wildebeest, kept Serengeti wildebeest few until wiped out there in the 1960s
checks.note: Holdo et al. 2009: the wildebeest irruption followed rinderpest eradication in the 1960s. Grokipedia (Rinderpest) records it decimating wildebeest in the 1890s.

checks.claim: Herds grew from about a quarter of a million to more than a million by the late 1970s
checks.note: About 250,000 in 1961 (Sinclair and Norton-Griffiths) to about 1.4 million (PBS; UBC: six-fold in about 15 years). Sinclair elsewhere recalls 'barely 200,000'; 'about a quarter of a million' is fair.

checks.claim: Key: trees rose as fewer fires swept the grazed grass
checks.note: The irruption 'led to a widespread reduction in the extent of fire and an ongoing recovery of the tree population'.

checks.claim: Wrong choices (herds ate trees; trampled seedlings; stayed the same)
checks.note: Wildebeest are grazers; tree density rose.

checks.claim: Context: fire kills small trees; Sinclair judged trees at levels not seen since the 1800s; Holdo's team tested elephants and rainfall and found fire explained the trees best
checks.note: Sinclair (arrived 1965): 'less fuel, and therefore less burning'; trees that 'probably hadn't occurred since the 1800's'. Holdo: elephants 'only weak support', rainfall 'failed to directly explain', fire 'the primary driver'.

checks.claim: Woodwell's team measured DDT along a food chain in a Long Island estuary in the 1960s
checks.note: Woodwell, Wurster and Isaacson, Science 156: 821-824 (1967), salt marsh and estuary on Long Island's south shore.

checks.claim: Plankton 0.04 ppm; small fish 0.5; larger fish 2; fish-eating birds such as ospreys about 25
checks.note: Paper's abstract: 0.04 ppm in plankton, birds 10-100 times fish, up to 75 ppm in a ring-billed gull. Stanford: 3-25 ppm in gulls, terns, cormorants, mergansers, herons and ospreys. The 0.5 / 2 / 25 chain is the rounded popular version (Time, 1969), consistent with the paper's ranges.

checks.claim: Water about 3 parts per trillion (0.000003 ppm), attributed to Woodwell's team
checks.note: The 3 ppt figure comes from Time 1969 (which does not name Woodwell and says Long Island Sound) and an unattributed Grokipedia line. A university teaching page built on Cox's textbook figure of the 1967 study gives water-to-zooplankton as 800x, which implies about 0.00005 ppm (50 ppt) in the paper. The primary table could not be read. Fix: drop the water figure from the stem ('The plankton held about 0.04 parts per million, small fish 0.5, larger fish 2, and fish-eating birds such as ospreys about 25.').

checks.claim: Context: 'by these numbers the level climbs more than eight million times from water to bird'
checks.note: Rests on the 3 ppt water figure; with the paper's apparent 0.00005 ppm it would be about 500,000 times. Fix: 'the level climbs more than six hundred times from plankton to bird' (0.04 to 25).

checks.claim: Key: each eater stores the DDT from its many meals
checks.note: Contaminants 'accumulate in fatty tissues and are retained due to slow elimination rates'; predators take in contaminants from many prey.

checks.claim: Wrong choices (more body; more spray; DDT multiplies)
checks.note: ppm is per unit of body weight, so size alone does not raise it; DDT is a chemical and does not reproduce.

checks.claim: Context: DDT fat-soluble, hardly water-soluble, slowly broken down; biomagnification; Carson's Silent Spring 1962
checks.note: Grokipedia: Silent Spring (1962) showed DDT's accumulation and transfer to higher predators.

checks.claim: Ratcliffe found broken peregrine eggs in Britain in the 1950s
checks.note: 1958 note in British Birds on 'the abnormal number of broken eggs he was finding in Peregrine eyries'.

checks.claim: He weighed and measured museum and private-collection eggs, some over a century old, and eggs from his own surveys
checks.note: Index = shell weight / (length x breadth); British Museum (Natural History) eggs and 30 recent survey eggs; JSTOR Daily: private collections too.

checks.claim: Key: steady for a century, then thinner from 1947 on
checks.note: 'a steady 1.82 for over 125 years'; 'the turning point in Britain was in 1947'; fell to 1.53, a 16% loss.

checks.claim: Wrong choices (gradual thinning; no thinning; from 1939)
checks.note: Thinning began abruptly in 1947 in Britain and the US; 1939 is the year DDT's insect-killing power was found.

checks.claim: Context: about a sixth thinner; DDT in mass use from 1945; insecticide action found 1939
checks.note: 16% is about a sixth; Müller 1939; farmers adopted it en masse from 1945.

checks.claim: Context: Hickey and Anderson found the same thinning in the US from 1947, in ospreys and bald eagles; captive kestrels fed DDE laid thinner shells
checks.note: Science 1968: thinning 'began in 1947', 19 percent or more, 'identical to phenomena reported in Britain'; three declining raptors (peregrine, bald eagle, osprey). Wiemeyer and Porter (Nature 1970) on kestrels.

checks.claim: Context: US DDT ban 1972; bald eagle nesting pairs in the lower 48 rose from 417 (1963) to 9,789 (2007), helped by protection from shooting
checks.note: FWS: all-time low of 417 nesting pairs in 1963; 9,789 breeding pairs at delisting in 2007; DDT banned 1972.

unit_notes: Checked 2026-11-26 against the web (Grokipedia first). Two small context overclaims (Q3 'more whales', Q4 'no natural enemies'), one coverage overclaim (Q5 'several times as much' for all four mammals), and one unverified water figure (Q9: 3 ppt is Time's 1969 popular number; the 1967 paper's own water value appears to be about 0.00005 ppm). Paine's 15-to-8 count is dated 'within a year' by SciAm, Scitable, Grokipedia and HHMI, though Wikipedia says three years; the key stands. Yellowstone wording is properly hedged and reflects the debate (Brice et al. 2022, NPS).
